title: Demand is what the student does
statement: A task's thinking demand is the operation a learner must perform to answer it, not its stem's verb, the skill it claims, its difficulty label or expected pass rate.
detail: Items whose evaluate, explain or justify stems reduced to matching text, and items that described a skill instead of exercising it, were passing an item evaluator. Its base rubric now says such verbs describe the cover, not the demand (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/_base_evaluation.txt`); its reading-and-writing rubric requires items to exercise the targeted skill, not describe it (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/prompts/question/sat_rw_evaluation.txt`); and a regression test fails vocabulary-in-context items that pair an everyday word with a direct synonym, since they test synonym recognition (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/tests/test_evaluator_prompt_rules_969.py`). An item's level should be tagged by the work it requires, and even an easy item needs some thinking.
against: the label effect was pilot-only and didn't generalize when stacked with other tricks, and the same rubric accepts recall where the curriculum's own definition of a level describes recall.

evidence.quote: Verbs like *evaluate / claim / analyze / explain / justify* in the question stem do **not** rescue the item — they describe the cover, not the actual cognitive demand.
Items must exercise the targeted SAT R&W substandard, not describe the substandard in the abstract.
Items that use a foundational everyday word and a direct synonym answer test synonym recognition rather than determining meaning in context, and should fail `curriculum_alignment`.
